title: Greensboro autism facility permanently closes; bankruptcy filing reveals six figure debt - NewsBreak
text:
By Cassie Fambro ,
1 hours ago GREENSBORO, N.C. (WGHP) — Lovely Day ABA and Autism Services has shut down after an insurance dispute led the owner, Sunrise ABA and Autism Services LLC., to file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy.
On the same day that Sunrise ABA filed for bankruptcy, founder Mamie Turner alerted employees and families that the Greensboro facility, which served about 100 families with specialized therapy and individualized care, was permanently closing, according to court records.
Billing issues uncovered The first signs of trouble were in May when a six-figure billing issue came to light, according to administrators at the facility. FOX8 toured the Greensboro facility that month after administrators reached out about an ongoing insurance dispute.
“We were like, ‘Why are the news people here?’ Nobody knew,” said Smith.
Former employees like Smith say they learned about the financial struggle from our story on May 5 , in which administrators revealed the six-figure billing issue dating back six months.
They closed Lovely Day briefly and reopened, before permanently shutting down mid-June.
Now, employees are waiting for paychecks.
Waiting on paychecks Former employee and behavioral technician J’Kariana Smith is among about 70 former employees who say they have not been paid in weeks.
“Some of them are single mothers. Somebody got put out of their house,” said Smith.
She said employees received an email on the 16th “with the subject ‘Saying goodbye.’”
We spoke to multiple employees waiting on paychecks who did not want to appear on camera.
We reached out to an attorney Turner hired, Samantha Brumbaugh, for comment on Wednesday afternoon. We had not received a response as of the time of publication.
Smith says they’ve also reached out to Brumbaugh for updates on potential payment.
“We’re calling, we are emailing and we aren’t getting a response,” said Smith.
Debt dispute Court documents show Sunrise ABA’s top three debtors are two credit card companies and the managed care organization Trillium Health Resources, to which they show a debt of $329,000.
Turner disputes the debt, claiming Trillium Resources owed her company for care administered.
We’ve reached out for information on the dispute more than a dozen times since May 5 and have received no response as of Wednesday evening.
Meanwhile, families have scrambled to find alternate care, and employees like Smith are hoping to find another role helping children.
“I want to be a voice for them and be like a helping hand for them, more than anybody,” said Smith.
We are awaiting comment from Brumbaugh, the attorney, as well as Trillium Health Resources.
